To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) SAI and PCI interact with deletion and stress assignment; (2) SAI and PC I in exclamative clauses, comparative clauses and sluiced clauses are subject to a constraint that is sensitive to the presence of a wh-word in the clause; (3) SAI in exclamative and comparative clauses, as well as PC I in sluiced clauses, are sensitive to the position of the subject in the clause; and (4) SAI and PCl interact with deletion

SAI and PC in these clauses interact at PF, that SAI and PI in these clauses are best analyzed as PF phenomena, and that the interaction between SAI and PCI at PF is evidence that at least one type of head-movement takes place after Spell-Out.

SAI and (some instances of) PCI in comparative and exclama- tive clauses interact with deletion at PF, that this interaction can be accounted for by assuming PF head movement, and that the evidence for PF head movement comes from the interaction of these phenomena with deletion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction of PF operations with head movement and the PF-interface.
a particular type of head movement, and its interface properties.
the interaction of PF operations and head movement in the mapping from LF to PF.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
head movement is PF interface.
the evidence for head-movement in these clauses is overwhelming, but the evidence for head movement at Spell-Out is still inconclusive.
head movement is PF-external.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SAI and PCIs in these clauses are the PF effects of the movement of the auxiliary and preposition respectively.
head movement in the PF interface is not only possible, but also necessary.
SAI and PCIs in these clauses are not subject to the PIC.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SAI and PCIs are not PF phenomena.
PF is an active component in the grammar.
there is no reason to believe that head movement must be limited to the derivation of LF, and that the PF interface may be an equally important locus for the effects of movement.
